purpose: Lenalidomide is used to treat certain blood cancers, including multiple myeloma (a cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow) and some types of myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), which affect how your bone marrow makes blood cells. It is also used for mantle cell lymphoma and follicular lymphoma. It helps slow or stop the growth of cancer cells and can improve your blood counts.
how_it_works: Lenalidomide works in a few ways to fight cancer. It helps your immune system recognize and attack cancer cells more effectively. It also cuts off the blood supply that tumors need to grow and directly interferes with the cancer cells ability to survive and multiply.
common_side_effects: Fatigue and weakness, low blood cell counts (which can cause anemia, increased risk of infection, or easy bruising and bleeding), diarrhea or constipation, nausea, muscle cramps, rash, swelling in the hands or feet, and shortness of breath. Blood clots in the legs or lungs can also occur.
warnings: This medication has serious risks. It can cause severe birth defects or death of an unborn baby, so it must never be taken during pregnancy. Both men and women must use reliable birth control and enroll in a special safety program called REMS before getting this medicine. It can also cause dangerous blood clots, low blood counts, liver problems, and rarely a second new cancer. You will need regular blood tests to monitor your safety while on this medication. Do not donate blood while taking this drug.
typical_dosing: Dosing depends on the condition being treated, your kidney function, and how well you tolerate the medication. A common starting dose for multiple myeloma is 25 mg taken by mouth once daily on days 1 through 21 of a 28-day cycle, then a week off. Your doctor may lower the dose if you have side effects or kidney problems. Always take it exactly as prescribed and do not crush or chew the capsules.
